start: Learn to separate retinal vascular, optic nerve, ocular, and cortical causes.

references.label: EyeWiki: Primary vs. Secondary Angle Closure Glaucoma

One eye only (monocular) - Vision loss i.question: Is there pain or discomfort in or around the eye?

Yes - there is pain or significant disco.question: Which best describes the pain or discomfort?

metadata.teachingPearl: Pain characteristics and associated symptoms help localize the pathology.

No - the vision loss is painless - No ey.question: Did the vision loss go away on its own, within a few minutes?

No - vision is still reduced or absent -.question: What best describes the vision loss?

metadata.teachingPearl: The character of the vision loss narrows the differential significantly.
Transient (self-resolving) vision loss has a distinct set of causes from persistent loss.
Pain localizes the pathology and separates vascular/retinal causes from inflammatory or pressure-related causes.

Both eyes (binocular) - Vision loss pres.question: Are there any other symptoms alongside the vision loss?

No other neurological symptoms - vision.question: How quickly did the vision loss develop?

metadata.teachingPearl: Onset speed helps distinguish vascular events from slower-developing pathology.
Associated neurological signs help localize the lesion and determine urgency.
Ask the patient to cover each eye alternately. Monocular loss indicates pathology anterior to the optic chiasm (ocular or optic nerve). Binocular loss points to retrochiasmal pathology (brain).

title: Flashes, Floaters, or Curtain
start: Learn to triage PVD vs retinal tear, retinal detachment, and vitreous hemorrhage.

node.question: Are the flashes/floaters new and clearly different from baseline?

Yes - this is new or clearly worsening -.question: Are there warning signs of retinal detachment?

No curtain or field defect - Vision is a.question: Is there pain, photophobia, or red eye?

No - painless and not significantly red.question: Are flashing lights present with the floaters?

Yes - clear new flashes are present - Li.question: Any high-risk factors for retinal tear or detachment?

metadata.teachingPearl: Recent trauma or surgery, high myopia, prior retinal tear/detachment, and sudden shower of floaters increase risk.

No flashes - Floaters are present withou.question: Which pattern best matches the visual symptom?

metadata.teachingPearl: Without flashes, pattern and associated features help separate migraine, hemorrhage, and stable benign floaters.
Photopsias suggest vitreoretinal traction and raise concern for retinal tear or detachment.
Pain and light sensitivity with floaters suggest inflammatory pathology rather than isolated vitreoretinal traction.
A curtain, dark shadow, or new peripheral field loss should be treated as detachment until proven otherwise.
New onset symptoms (hours to weeks) carry retinal risk. Longstanding stable floaters without change are usually lower risk.

title: Red or Painful Eye
start: Learn high-yield red-eye differentiators: keratitis, uveitis, scleritis, angle closure, conjunctivitis, dry eye.

references.label: EyeWiki: Primary vs. Secondary Angle Closure Glaucoma
NIH/NEI: Omega-3s from fish oil supplements no better than placebo for dry eye

node.question: Is there pain in or around the red eye - beyond mild grittiness or scratchiness?

Yes - there is true pain (aching, severe.question: Is vision blurred or noticeably reduced?

metadata.teachingPearl: When pain AND vision change occur together in a red eye, the diagnosis is almost always serious. These next questions identify the specific emergent or urgent cause.

No - vision seems normal or is only mini.question: How would you describe the severity and quality of the pain?

metadata.teachingPearl: Pain character reliably separates scleritis (a systemic disease marker) from episcleritis (benign and self-limited). This distinction determines urgency significantly.
Any vision change alongside pain in a red eye significantly elevates the urgency - angle-closure glaucoma, keratitis, and uveitis all present this way.

No - no true pain (mild grittiness or ir.question: Is there any noticeable discharge from the eye?

Yes - there is discharge (watery, sticky.question: What type of discharge is present?

metadata.teachingPearl: Discharge character is one of the highest-yield differentiating features in the painless red eye. This single observation reliably separates bacterial from viral etiology.

No - no significant discharge - Eye is r.question: What is the dominant symptom or finding?

metadata.teachingPearl: In a painless red eye without discharge, the nature of the symptom and the appearance of the redness guide the diagnosis.
In the painless red eye, the presence and character of discharge is the first key branching point.

The presence and severity of pain is the single highest-yield initial question in evaluating a red eye. True pain (aching, deep, or severe) strongly predicts serious pathology. Mild grittiness or foreign-body sensation without true pain is considered 'no pain' for this question.

title: Eye Trauma or Chemical Exposure
start: Learn emergency trauma triage: open globe, chemical burn, hyphema, orbital fracture, corneal injury.

node.question: Was there a chemical splash or chemical exposure to the eye?

No - this was a physical injury (blunt,.question: What was the mechanism of injury?

Blunt trauma - fist, ball, airbag, fall,.question: Are any of these signs present that suggest the eye may be open?

No - none of these signs are present; ey.question: Is the orbit tense or bulging, with significant vision loss?

No - orbit may be bruised and swollen, b.question: What is the most prominent finding after the blunt trauma?

metadata.teachingPearl: With the globe confirmed closed and no orbital compartment syndrome, these findings help identify the specific injury pattern.

Proptosis (forward globe protrusion) plus an afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) after orbital trauma signals orbital compartment syndrome - a true emergency requiring immediate canthotomy within 90 minutes.
An open globe must be identified immediately to prevent any further pressure on the eye. Stop the examination as soon as any of these signs are found.

Penetrating, sharp, or foreign body - kn.question: What was the nature and velocity of the foreign body or penetrating object?

metadata.teachingPearl: High-velocity mechanisms (grinding, chiseling, drilling, nailing without eye protection) can create self-sealing wounds that look normal on exam but conceal an intraocular foreign body - CT is mandatory.
Mechanism guides the next steps. Blunt trauma and penetrating/foreign-body mechanisms have different priority assessments and management pathways.

Chemical injury is the highest-priority triage question in eye trauma - irrigation must begin IMMEDIATELY, before any other assessment. Even a 30-second delay worsens the injury. If chemical exposure occurred, begin irrigation now.

title: Neuro-Ophthalmic Signs
start: Learn pupil emergencies, diplopia localization, papilledema, optic neuropathy, and cavernous sinus/orbital apex syndromes.

references.label: EyeWiki: Non-Arteritic Anterior Ischemic Optic Neuropathy

Abnormal pupil or anisocoria.question: What is the main pupillary concern?

Unequal pupil size (anisocoria) - One pu.question: In which lighting is anisocoria more noticeable?

metadata.teachingPearl: When anisocoria is greater in bright light, the larger pupil is usually abnormal (parasympathetic pathway).
When anisocoria is greater in dim light, the smaller pupil is usually abnormal (sympathetic pathway).
Lighting response helps identify whether the large or small pupil is pathologic.

Abnormal light reaction with similar pup.question: What is the main reaction abnormality?

metadata.teachingPearl: If pupil size is not the main issue, focus on afferent defects and light-near dissociation patterns.
Start by separating anisocoria (size difference) from reaction abnormalities. Any acute painful eye, ptosis, diplopia, or neurologic deficit raises urgency.

Double vision or ocular motility problem.question: Cover each eye separately: does the double vision persist when ONE eye is covered?

No - double vision resolves when either.question: Is there ptosis (a drooping eyelid) on one side?

Yes - one upper eyelid is clearly droopi.question: Is the ptosis or diplopia fatigable - clearly worse with sustained gaze or at the end of the day?

No - constant and non-fluctuating - Ptos.question: Is the pupil on the droopy-eyelid side LARGER than the other and sluggish to light?

metadata.teachingPearl: Pupillary involvement is the critical variable in CN III palsy. A dilated, non-reactive pupil means parasympathetic fiber compression - the hallmark of aneurysmal or compressive CN III palsy. Equal, reactive pupils suggest microvascular ischemia.

Fatigability is the hallmark of neuromuscular junction disorders like myasthenia gravis. Ask: 'Is it worse after reading for a while, or worse at night than in the morning?' Improvement after rest or sleep is equally important.

No ptosis - both eyelids are at their no.question: In which direction are the two images mainly separated?

Horizontal - images side by side - Worse.question: Can the affected eye move fully inward (toward the nose)?

metadata.teachingPearl: For horizontal diplopia: test adduction by asking the patient to follow your finger toward their nose from the side. Failure to adduct with nystagmus in the other eye = INO. Failure to abduct (outward) with inward drift at rest = CN VI.

Vertical - one image above the other, or.question: Is there proptosis (bulging eye), eyelid retraction, or a known history of thyroid disease?

metadata.teachingPearl: Thyroid eye disease causes restrictive strabismus and vertical diplopia from enlarged fibrotic extraocular muscles (inferior rectus most commonly). CN IV palsy is the other main cause of vertical diplopia - look for head tilt and worse diplopia when looking down.

Ask the patient: 'Are the two images side by side (horizontal), one above the other (vertical), or does the double vision come and go inconsistently?' The direction helps localize the responsible muscle or nerve.

Ptosis with diplopia narrows the differential significantly: CN III palsy and myasthenia gravis both cause ptosis + ophthalmoplegia. If there is no ptosis, the pattern of double vision directs the workup.

This single test separates eye problems (monocular diplopia) from brain and cranial nerve problems (binocular diplopia). Ask the patient to cover the right eye - is double vision still present? Then cover the left eye - is it still present? Binocular diplopia resolves when EITHER eye is covered.

Disc edema, optic neuropathy, nystagmus,.question: What is the primary neuro-ophthalmic concern?

Bilateral disc swelling found on fundosc.question: Are there features that point toward raised intracranial pressure?

Yes - headache, pulsatile tinnitus, dipl.question: Are the visual episodes brief seconds-long obscurations rather than prolonged monocular loss?

metadata.teachingPearl: Seconds-long graying or blacking out with posture change fits TVOs; prolonged loss suggests a different vascular or retinal process.

No - bilateral elevated discs were found.question: Does the disc appearance look like true edema rather than a crowded or lumpy congenital disc?

metadata.teachingPearl: True papilledema is more likely when there is vessel obscuration, hyperemia, hemorrhage, or cotton-wool spots. Small crowded lumpy discs without those features suggest pseudopapilledema.
Think headache worse when lying flat, pulsatile tinnitus, CN VI palsy, nausea, positional worsening, or transient visual obscurations.

Subacute optic neuropathy with pain on e.question: Does the presentation fit typical unilateral demyelinating optic neuritis?

Yes - typical unilateral painful optic n.question: Are any atypical optic neuritis features present?

metadata.teachingPearl: Examples: bilateral or recurrent loss, severe disc edema or hemorrhage, poor recovery, uveitis/retinitis, systemic autoimmune or infectious clues.

Typical cases are unilateral, painful with eye movement, evolve over hours to days, and occur in younger adults. Bilateral, recurrent, fulminant, hemorrhagic, infectious, or inflammatory cases are atypical.

Older patient with acute optic neuropath.question: Are there convincing arteritic or systemic inflammatory clues?

No - older patient with painless optic n.question: Does the case fit a classic NAION profile?

metadata.teachingPearl: Think painless monocular loss, crowded swollen disc, altitudinal defect, vascular risk factors, and no pain with eye movement.
Ask about jaw claudication, scalp tenderness, new headache, PMR symptoms, constitutional symptoms, or known inflammatory marker elevation.

Painful ophthalmoplegia or multiple cran.question: Are there venous congestion or flow-related clues such as corkscrew vessels, bruit, pulsation, or trauma?

metadata.teachingPearl: Visual loss, RAPD, color desaturation, or optic disc edema/atrophy point to orbital apex syndrome rather than isolated cavernous sinus syndrome.
Those findings strongly suggest carotid-cavernous fistula rather than a generic cavernous sinus process.

Nystagmus or other rhythmic abnormal eye.question: Did the nystagmus begin in infancy or early childhood?

No - this is new or acquired - Now decid.question: Is the pattern clearly peripheral vestibular?

No - not clearly peripheral - Check for.question: Is there a strong medication, substance, or toxic-metabolic explanation?

metadata.teachingPearl: Think anticonvulsants, lithium, sedatives, alcohol, or other intoxication with gaze-evoked bidirectional nystagmus and ataxia.
A peripheral pattern is usually unidirectional horizontal-torsional, associated with vertigo, suppressed by fixation, and paired with an abnormal head impulse test.
Early-onset nystagmus follows a pediatric eye-development pathway. New nystagmus in older children or adults is a different problem.
Pick the dominant bedside pattern first, then narrow the localization.
Learn pupil emergencies, diplopia localization, papilledema, optic neuropathy, and cavernous sinus/orbital apex syndromes.

title: Eyelid or Periorbital Swelling
start: Learn eyelid/orbit triage: preseptal vs orbital cellulitis, chalazion, hordeolum, dacryocystitis, blepharitis.

metadata.teachingPearl: Check for proptosis, restricted eye movements, decreased visual acuity, or pain with eye movements. These distinguish orbital from preseptal cellulitis.

Focal bump or nodule on the eyelid - Dis.question: Is the bump acutely painful and erythematous?

metadata.teachingPearl: Distinguish between acute infection (hordeolum) and chronic granuloma (chalazion).

Eyelid rash - itchy, scaly, or eczematou.question: Are there clustered vesicles on the eyelid skin?

metadata.teachingPearl: Vesicular clusters suggest herpetic etiology; diffuse eczematous changes suggest contact or atopic dermatitis.
Assess the dominant eyelid/periorbital finding on initial evaluation.

metadata.teachingPearl: A visible lens opacity suggests cataract, but any posterior white reflex or uncertainty still requires urgent retinoblastoma-focused evaluation.

Visible eye crossing or abnormal corneal.question: What is the pattern of the apparent eye misalignment?

metadata.teachingPearl: Age of onset, corneal light reflex symmetry, and abrupt neurologic symptoms help separate pseudostrabismus from urgent acquired strabismus.

Normal external exam and red reflex, but.question: How strong is the amblyopia-risk pattern?

metadata.teachingPearl: Repeated failure, inter-eye asymmetry, or known anisometropia / strabismus should be treated more seriously than a single borderline screen.
The first step is separating isolated screening failure from structural red flags such as leukocoria, strabismus, corneal opacity, or deprivation.

title: Gradual or Chronic Vision Change
start: Learn common outpatient patterns: cataract, dry eye, AMD, glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy, presbyopia.

references.label: NIH/NEI: Omega-3s from fish oil supplements no better than placebo for dry eye

node.question: What best describes the main visual complaint?

Blurry or hazy vision - gradual onset ov.question: Is there a history of diabetes, or has the blur worsened more suddenly recently?

metadata.teachingPearl: Diabetic retinopathy can cause blurring through macular edema even before PDR develops. In older adults without diabetes, gradual painless blur over years is most commonly a cataract.

Straight lines look wavy or distorted (m.question: How quickly did the waviness or distortion of straight lines appear?

metadata.teachingPearl: The speed of onset distinguishes urgent wet AMD (sudden neovascularization) from slowly progressive dry AMD. Any recent change in a known AMD patient - even subtle - should be triaged as urgent.

Halos around lights or difficulty with n.question: Are there also any peripheral vision changes, or a family history of glaucoma?

metadata.teachingPearl: Halos and glare from cataracts are very common. However, halos can also occur in glaucoma. The key differentiating feature is peripheral (side) vision loss - which only occurs in glaucoma, not cataracts.

This module covers gradual or chronic visual symptoms - common conditions seen in primary care and routine checkups. For sudden vision loss or flashes, use the Acute Vision Loss or Flashes & Floaters modules.

title: Approach to Strabismus (Squint)
start: Learn to differentiate pseudostrabismus, esotropia, and exotropia.

node.question: Is the eye turning IN (Esotropia) or OUT (Exotropia)?

Turning IN (Esotropia).question: When did the inward turning start?

metadata.teachingPearl: Determine the direction of deviation (eso vs exo) and the onset to narrow down the diagnosis.

title: Binocular Single Vision (BSV) & Sensory Adaptations
start: Detailed evaluation of sensory anomalies including Suppression, Amblyopia, and Anomalous Retinal Correspondence (ARC).

node.question: Perform the Worth 4-Dot (W4D) test. What does the patient report seeing?

4 Dots (1 Red, 2 Green, 1 Mixed).question: Does the patient have a manifest strabismus on cover test?

metadata.teachingPearl: If a patient has a manifest tropia but sees 4 dots, they have Anomalous Retinal Correspondence (ARC). Their brain has remapped the macula to avoid diplopia.
Normal Binocular Single Vision (BSV) with Normal Retinal Correspondence (NRC).
Left Eye Suppression. The brain is ignoring the image from the left eye to prevent diplopia.
Right Eye Suppression. The brain is ignoring the image from the right eye.

5 Dots (2 Red, 3 Green).question: Where are the red dots located relative to the green dots?

metadata.teachingPearl: Uncrossed diplopia indicates Esotropia (convergent squint). The visual axes cross in front of the object.
Crossed diplopia indicates Exotropia (divergent squint). The visual axes cross behind the object.
The Worth 4-Dot test requires red/green glasses (red over right eye usually). It is the gold standard for rapidly identifying suppression, diplopia, and ARC.

title: Paralytic & Restrictive Strabismus
start: Differentiating cranial nerve palsies (3rd, 4th, 6th) from restrictive myopathies (Duane, Brown, TED).

node.question: In which direction is the gaze limitation most severe?

Abduction (Looking outward towards the e.question: Is there globe retraction and narrowing of the palpebral fissure on adduction?

metadata.teachingPearl: Duane Retraction Syndrome (Type 1 is most common: limited abduction). Caused by paradoxical co-contraction of medial and lateral recti.
6th Cranial Nerve (Abducens) Palsy. The lateral rectus muscle is weak. Esotropia worsens on gaze toward the affected side.
Brown Syndrome (Superior Oblique Tendon Sheath Syndrome). The SO tendon cannot slide through the trochlea, restricting the IO's ability to pull the eye up and in.

Complex limitation (Cannot look up, down.question: Is the pupil dilated and unreactive to light?

metadata.teachingPearl: Pupil-involving 3rd Nerve Palsy is a medical emergency! Highly suspicious for a posterior communicating (PCoA) artery aneurysm compressing the superficial pupillary fibers.
Pupil-sparing 3rd Nerve Palsy is typically microvascular/ischemic (diabetes, hypertension). The deep motor fibers are infarcted but superficial pupillary fibers survive.
Always differentiate a true neurological palsy from mechanical restriction using Forced Duction Testing.
